title: The Pilot's Price
passages:
The season bell hung off the Kettle's low gate, bronze and pitted and older than anybody's grandmother, and it rang the tide whether the raft-city wanted it or not. Sol stood under it with her chin up, counting.

The gate kid on the hammer was eleven, maybe, and had a cold. He struck the quarter, skipped one, banged twice fast to catch up.

"Again," Sol said. "From the half. Don't get clever."

"He's sick," Wren said.

"He's got a job."

The second time came out clean, and the note went flat across the water, across the lashed rafts and the salvaged hulls and the drowned tops of the old city standing in the swell like bad teeth. North of the gate the sky had gone the color of an old bruise, stacked in shelves from the water up past where you could look. Nobody mentioned it. Everybody looked.

Wren had the slate in her hands — the one she'd pulled off Salas — and wasn't playing it. Just holding it.

"Slack water," Sol said, "is the twenty minutes at the turn when the tide quits pushing. Stops dead. That's the only stretch the Stair lets a hull through, because for twenty minutes the drowned streets aren't a river." She counted it out on her fingers, strokes of the bell. "Half past ten to eleven by the kid's count. Slack at eleven-oh-eight. The bell seals the Stair at slack, and once it turns, the water comes back down that channel hard enough to fold the Marrow like a wet crate."

"So we go at eleven-oh-eight," Dey said.

"We go at eleven-oh-eight, and Mercy General stays shut behind us until the season turns. Four months of Nia and Teo breathing on somebody else's charity."

Teo was asleep against Nia's hip with the blanket over his ears. Nia didn't look up. "She's not dead."

"Nobody said dead."

"People keep saying it with their faces."

Dey shifted his weight, careful, still learning to breathe like a man who owned his own lungs. "Four hours to go ask a bell why it's hollering through a dead man's throat. Wonderful. I'll get my good boots."

"You'll get your good boots and stay topside," Sol said. "Bayo takes the channel. I take the helm."

Wren's head came up. "Sol."

"Both. His voice in my ear, my hands on the wheel, the way it's been since before any of you could swim." She said it evenly. The evenness was worse than shouting. "I'm not giving my boat to a man with no bell-mark, no berth, and a promise in his mouth. I'm letting him talk me through water I can't see. There's a difference, and I'll thank you to remember it."

Salas sat on the winch drum with his forearms on his knees, watching all of it, saying nothing, which was most of what he did now.

"Eleven-oh-eight is the whole margin," Wren said. "If that kid's cold gets worse—"

"Then I'll take the hammer off him myself."

Sol climbed to the wheelhouse, lifted the chalk off its nail, and wrote it on the bulkhead by the door. ELEVEN-oh-eight. She always wrote the slack up there. She'd told Wren once that a number on a wall doesn't drown.

Wren came up behind her and stopped.

There were four more times on that bulkhead under hers, same square hand. Four slacks, each with a tally beside it, and the chalk on the last had been gone over twice, pressed hard, the way a hand writes when it doesn't trust itself.

"Whose are those?"

Sol looked at them a while. Long enough that Wren heard the bell kid strike the quarter again below.

"Mine," Sol said. "That's my hand. I wrote those."

"You don't remember."

"I remember eleven-oh-eight." Sol set the chalk back on the nail, square in the same worn spot, without looking for it. "That's the only one that matters today."

Below, on the deck, Bayo had stopped coiling. The line hung slack in his fists and he was looking up at the wheelhouse glass, doing arithmetic of his own.

Sol came down the ladder slow, which was how the crew always knew.

Wren came after her with the slate held against her chest in both hands, the way you carry something that might get up and walk.

"Say it again," Wren said. "Slower. His voice or your hands. I want to know which one I'm putting in the log."

"I heard me."

"Everyone heard you. Dey has good ears and bad lungs."

"Free crew," Dey said from the rail, hauling on his good boots. "I get opinions now. It's in the book."

"It's not in the book."

Sol stopped in front of Bayo. He had the coil going again, laying it flat across his palm, a neat job, the kind you hang on a nail instead of dropping on the deck.

"Bayo."

"Captain."

"I've run the Stair once, and you were up on the bell telling me where the corners were." She said it to him and not to the planking. "You've got no mark now. You can't be a voice out of the sky. So I need you standing on my boards with your mouth going and both hands free."

"You need me on the wheel."

"I need you on the wheel."

The gate kid struck the quarter above them and the note went out flat across the rafts.

"Sol," Wren said.

"Not now."

"He cut a man's line clean and left him sitting in the dark fourteen months. Quill read it out at the low gate with everyone listening."

"I was standing there. I know whose line he cut." Sol didn't turn around. "That isn't the question. The question is whether he knows the water, and he's the only pilot breathing who does. I'm not taking my people down there on a guess because I'd rather keep my pride dry."

Then she dropped her voice, which meant it was meant for him and Wren got it anyway.

"There are four slacks chalked on my wall in my own hand and I can't account for one of them. Chalk doesn't drown and a number doesn't either, but I can't tell you what I did in those hours or who I did it with." A beat. "I'm not putting this crew through a hole in the world on a wheel I don't remember turning."

Wren's mouth opened and shut. She had rebuilt lost hours with her own hands and she knew exactly whose wall that was, and she said nothing, which was its own kind of answer.

Bayo laid the last of the coil across his palm and looked at it.

"Twenty minutes," he said.

"Twenty. Your voice the whole way down, no gaps, no guessing. Your hands if it goes bad. I stand at your shoulder and I keep my mouth shut unless I have to open it."

"And the Marrow?"

"The Marrow's mine. The wheel's yours till the turn." She let that sit where everyone could see it. "You want it written, I'll walk down to the counter and have Quill enter it in front of you. She can't lie. It'll be true."

"He wants a page with his name on it," Dey said. "Before the bell shuts the channel."

"Nobody asked the boots."

Bayo opened his mouth.

"Mara."

It came off the winch drum, low and cracked and patient, the voice of a man talking to keep himself breathing. Salas hadn't moved. Forearms on his knees, eyes down.

Nobody said anything. Nia's head came up for the first time all morning. Teo shifted against her hip and slept on.

"Say that again," Nia said.

"Mara." Same spacing, same shape, the exact cadence of it coming out of the little slate in Wren's hands. "She's still singing."

Nia's face went flat and hard, the way it did when she was counting out medicine. "She never sang. Singing is air. You don't spend air on singing when there's a boy in a cold-case who needs it."

Salas looked up at her then, and his mouth worked around something that wasn't there anymore.

And Bayo, who had not said one word about the wheel, still didn't say one.

Bayo's mouth moved, shaped around something that wasn't the word yes, wasn't the word no, just air moving through a throat that had gotten good at making promises sound like weather.

"Twenty minutes," he said again, slower now, like he was tasting it. "Slack at eleven-oh-eight. I'll walk you down the Stair and back. My voice, your hands, both of us breathing when the bell strikes."

Sol didn't nod. Didn't shake. Just watched his face the way she watched a line under load, waiting for the first strand to sing.

"Your hands if it goes bad," she said. "You said that."

"I did."

"And the Marrow stays mine."

"The Marrow stays yours."

"Quill writes it."

"Quill writes it."

He said it all with the same easy warmth he used on the bell rope, calling the tide to the rafts that couldn't read it for themselves. A voice that made you believe the water would hold you up.

Salas hadn't looked away. Fourteen months in an air pocket at forty-two meters had carved the fat off his face and left the bone showing clean, but his eyes were the same eyes that had watched Bayo's knife come down through the ascent line, clean and deliberate, the way you cut a rope when you've already decided the man on the other end isn't coming up.

Bayo's face didn't change. Not a flicker at the jaw, not a widening around the eyes. He'd had fourteen months to practice the face that went with the promise, and he wore it like a second skin.

*I won't be there to hold it,* the face said, quiet as the slack water. *I'll talk you down. I'll talk you up. But when the strain comes, my hands will be on something else.*

He coiled the last of the line, neat and precise, and hung it on the pin by the wheelhouse door. A pilot's line, on a pilot's pin, on a boat he didn't own with a mark he didn't have.

"Eleven-oh-eight," he said to the bulkhead chalk. "We leave on the half."
